subject: ss-neurosurgery
title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap, grades, Fisher vasospasm and securing
refs: AHA/ASA Guideline for Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Haemorrhage 2023

steps.say: A ruptured aneurysm is striking like a thunderclap with peak pain in seconds. Vomiting with a stiff neck and sensitivity to light are completing the picture. A milder warning headache days earlier is reported by a third of patients.
steps.tx: A ruptured aneurysm presents with a **thunderclap headache** peaking within seconds, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and loss of consciousness, while a milder sentinel leak headache days earlier occurs in a third of patients. The onset is abrupt and maximal at onset, unlike migraine build-up. Any first severe headache of this kind is worked up as a bleed until proven otherwise.

rows: Warns in a third of patients

steps.say: The WFNS scale is grading by coma score with deficit from grade one to five. The Hunt-Hess scale is running from mild headache to coma across the same five grades. Both scales are predicting outcome and timing of surgery.
steps.tx: The **WFNS scale** grades SAH by Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) from grade I (GCS 15) to grade V (GCS 3 to 6 regardless of deficit), with focal deficit separating grade II from grade III at GCS 13 to 14, and the Hunt-Hess scale runs from grade I mild headache to grade V coma, both predicting outcome and timing of surgery. A higher grade means a sicker brain and a poorer prognosis. Grading is repeated because early scores can worsen quickly.

rows: GCS 13 to 14, deficit only in III

steps.say: The modified Fisher grade is reading vasospasm risk from the CT blood load. Thin blood without ventricular spill is carrying the lowest risk. Thick cisternal blood with ventricular blood is carrying the highest delayed ischaemia risk.
steps.tx: The **modified Fisher** grade predicts vasospasm from the CT blood load: thin SAH without ventricular blood is lowest risk while thick cisternal blood with intraventricular blood carries the highest delayed ischaemia risk. Blood volume on the first scan therefore sets the watch level. Heavy-load patients receive the closest neuromonitoring.

vis.caption: Ruptured berry aneurysm with subarachnoid blood, vasospasm and star-pattern CT clot. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: About a third of aneurysms are sitting at the anterior communicating artery. Posterior communicating and middle cerebral bifurcation sites are following next. Smoking with hypertension, family history and polycystic kidneys are raising the risk.
steps.tx: About 30 percent of aneurysms sit at the **anterior communicating artery**, with posterior communicating and middle cerebral bifurcation next, and risk factors are smoking, hypertension, family history and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Screening is offered to first-degree relatives in familial clusters. Modifiable risks are counselled at every visit.

vis.alt: Circle of Willis diagram with saccular aneurysms at branch points including the anterior communicating artery, one shown ruptured with subarachnoid blood.
vis.caption: Saccular aneurysms at Circle of Willis branch points with anterior communicating site commonest. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Noncontrast CT is near perfect within six hours of onset but sensitivity is falling after a day. A negative late scan with strong suspicion is needing a lumbar puncture. Yellow xanthochromia after twelve hours or CTA is confirming the bleed.
steps.tx: Noncontrast CT is near perfect within 6 hours of onset but sensitivity falls after a day, so a negative late CT with strong suspicion needs **lumbar puncture** showing xanthochromia after 12 hours or CTA (CT angiography). Xanthochromia is yellow bilirubin pigment from lysed red cells. Never accept one negative test when the story shouts bleed.

nodes.label: Negative but suspected: LP or CTA

steps.say: CTA is chosen first once CT has shown blood because it is fast and widely available. DSA is remaining the gold standard for small, blister and treatment-planning detail. Every bleed is getting urgent vessel imaging to find the culprit.
steps.tx: CTA (CT angiography) is the first-line vessel study on a positive CT while DSA (digital subtraction angiography) remains the **gold standard** for small, blister and treatment-planning detail, and every SAH gets vessel imaging urgently to find the bleeder. CTA maps the aneurysm neck and branches for the treatment choice. DSA adds dynamic flow detail when CTA is equivocal.

steps.say: Rebleeding is peaking in the first day with death above half per episode. Teams are securing the aneurysm as early as feasible once diagnosed. Blood pressure is controlled meanwhile without dropping brain perfusion.
steps.tx: Rebleeding risk peaks in the first 24 hours with mortality above 50 percent per rebleed, so teams **secure the aneurysm** as early as feasible and blood pressure is controlled without dropping cerebral perfusion. Antifibrinolytics are a bridge only when securing is delayed. Every hour unsecured is counted as risk.

steps.say: Acute hydrocephalus from ventricular blood with a falling score is needing an external drain. Chronic communicating hydrocephalus is developing later in about a fifth of survivors. A permanent shunt is placed when dependency is proven.
steps.tx: Acute hydrocephalus from intraventricular blood with a falling GCS needs an **external ventricular drain**, and chronic communicating hydrocephalus later needs a permanent shunt in about a fifth of survivors. The drain is weaned by gradual raising and clamping trials. Persistent need proves shunt dependency.

right.title: Permanent shunt (chronic)
points: Placed in a fifth of survivors
